headlines.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.
headlines.article_text: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. Amazon Web Services said it was "operating normally" and noted inaccurate reports of outages on its platforms. Google users reported issues on DownDetector. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A sign on the Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington, US, Oct. 26, 2026. David Ryder | Reuters Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday that impacted users around the world. The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. External services that connect with Outlook features such as Calendar also experienced issues. Email and other tools were unavailable for Microsoft users through much of the Asian business day and into the early European hours. In an update just before 6:20 a.m. in London (1:20 a.m. ET), Microsoft said "Users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services," including Outlook on either web or desktop, and did not give a timeline for restoring service. "As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident. We will continue to treat this incident with urgency and priority until full resolution," Microsoft said, adding that it would provide a full report with further details once the problem was mitigated. It also said that as part of efforts to recover its frontend service, it was "evaluating traffic controls that can be applied to increase capacity and stability." Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data." At 4 p.m. Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online. "We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses." Microsoft initially said infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions" was responsible for the connectivity problems. The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure" and that some servers were failing automated health checks. "We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service," Microsoft wrote .
